{{Short description|Tree in set theory}}
A '''Jech–Kunen tree''' is a [[Tree (set theory)|set-theoretic tree]] with properties that are incompatible with the [[generalized continuum hypothesis]]. It is named after [[Thomas Jech]] and [[Kenneth Kunen]], both of whom studied the possibility and consequences of its existence.

==Definition==
In set theory, a [[Tree (set theory)|tree]] is a [[partially ordered set]] in which the predecessors of any element form a [[well-ordering]]. The height of any element is the [[order type]] of this well-ordering, and the height of the tree is the least [[ordinal number]] that exceeds the height of all elements. A ''branch'' of a tree is a maximal well-ordered subset. A ''ω''<sub>1</sub>-tree is a tree with [[cardinality]] <math>\aleph_1</math> and height ''ω''<sub>1</sub>, where ''ω''<sub>1</sub> is the [[first uncountable ordinal]] and <math>\aleph_1</math> is the associated [[cardinal number]]. A Jech–Kunen tree is a ''ω''<sub>1</sub>-tree in which the number of branches is greater than <math>\aleph_1</math> and less than <math>2^{\aleph_1}</math>.

==Existence==
The [[generalized continuum hypothesis]] implies that there is no [[cardinal number]] between <math>\aleph_1</math> and <math>2^{\aleph_1}</math>; when this is the case, a Jech–Kunen tree cannot exist, because it is required to have a number of branches strictly between these two numbers.
{{harvs|txt|first=Thomas|last=Jech|authorlink=Thomas Jech|year=1971}} found the first [[Model theory|model]] in which this tree exists, and {{harvs|txt|first=Kenneth|last=Kunen|authorlink=Kenneth Kunen|year=1975}} showed that, assuming the [[continuum hypothesis]] and <math>2^{\aleph_1} > \aleph_2</math> , the existence of a Jech–Kunen tree is equivalent to the existence of a compact [[Hausdorff space]] with [[Base (topology)#Definition and basic properties|weight]] <math>\aleph_1</math> and cardinality strictly between <math>\aleph_1</math> and  <math>2^{\aleph_1}</math>.
